sections.body:
An online scam is a deception carried out over a digital channel, aimed at making you hand over money, credentials, or something else of value. It is not a rare and technical attack. Most of them are messages, and most of them are readable by anyone who knows what to look for.

What makes them work is not technical genius. It is **pressure**. A scam message tries to create a state where you act before you think: a parcel is waiting, an account will be closed in one hour, a prize must be claimed today, a family member is in trouble. Every one of those is designed to raise the cost of pausing.

That is why the usual advice to "be careful" fails. Carefulness is a state of mind, and pressure removes it. The scammer knows this, so the message builds the pressure for you. You do not have to defeat the pressure. You have to interrupt it.

The second thing to understand is **authority impersonation**. Scammers borrow the identity of institutions you already trust: a bank, a courier, a government office, a company you buy from, a colleague, a family member. Because the message arrives in a familiar tone, on a familiar-looking service, and with a plausible request, the first reaction is compliance rather than doubt.

The third thing is that **scams are now cheap to send at scale**. Generative writing means a message in your own language, in a natural tone, in seconds. A voice call in the local accent, in your language, at the right hour, is no longer a specialist trick. So the old assumption that a scam is obvious because of bad writing no longer holds, and the reliable signals are structural rather than stylistic.

Notice what this gives you. If the writing can be perfect, you cannot rely on writing. You rely on structure: where the message wants you to go, who it says it is, what it wants you to do, and whether you can verify it through a channel you chose yourself.

And one last thing. Being targeted is not a verdict on your intelligence. These messages are built to be convincing and they are sent to millions of people at once. Professionals fall for them. The difference between the people who recover and the people who do not is almost never intelligence. It is whether they had a procedure ready.
examples: The message was well written. That is exactly the point.
I was not careless. The message had built the pressure for me before I noticed it.
The scam did not rely on me being stupid. It relied on me being busy.
sections.heading: What an online scam is, and why it works on ordinary people

sections.body:
Scam messages look endless, but the structures underneath are few. Learn these four and most of them become readable at a glance.

Pattern one: the impersonation. You receive something that appears to come from someone you trust: your bank, a courier, a marketplace, a tax office, a colleague. The aim is to get you to act inside a trusted channel, which is why these arrive in your real inbox or through a real account of someone you know. The tell is that it wants you to move to a different channel: reply to this email, click here, call this number, install this app.

Pattern two: the urgent opportunity. A prize, a refund, a payment waiting, a job offer, an investment, a discount that ends tonight. The mechanics vary but the emotion is the same: a gain that will vanish if you hesitate.

Pattern three: the fabricated problem. A failed payment, a locked account, a suspicious login, a parcel held at customs, a family member who has lost their phone. This is the most effective pattern, because the natural reaction is to fix the problem, and fixing it involves following the message's instructions.

Pattern four: the harvest. You are moved to a page that looks real and asks for a password, a one-time code, a card number, a transfer, or a download. This is where the money or the data goes.

Patterns one and three combine more often than not, which is why they are the most dangerous: a trusted identity plus a problem that needs fixing today.

There is a fifth pattern worth naming even though it is not a scam in the same sense: the **advance fee**. A request for money before any service is delivered, from a supposed employer, landlord, supplier or love interest. The signature is that the fee always moves forward. Each payment is explained by the last one.
examples: It claimed to be my bank, and then asked me to call a number in the message.
The prize was generous, and it had to be claimed before midnight.
Each time I paid, there was a further charge. That is the signature.
sections.heading: The four patterns behind almost every scam

sections.body:
When a message arrives, read it against this list in order. The order matters, because the earliest signals are the most reliable and the cheapest to check. Most fake messages fail at the first two, and you can stop there.

Start with the sender identity, then the destination, then the request, then the tone. A message that passes the first three can still be a scam, but you will have done the work that matters.
sections.heading: The signals to check, in the order that saves the most time

symbols.meaning: A sender address that does not match the organisation it claims to be. Look at the real domain, not the display name, and check for extra characters or a different spelling.
A link whose destination is not the organisation it names. On a phone, long-press the link to see the address before you open it.
A phone number in the message instead of the number printed on your card or on the official website. A number you were given by a stranger is never a verification.
A request to move to another channel: reply to this email, install this app, join this chat, call this number. Legitimate organisations do not need you to leave their channel.
A request for a one-time code, a PIN, a password, or a card number. No legitimate organisation asks for these by message, ever.
Time pressure of any kind: an account closing in an hour, a payment to avoid a penalty, a prize expiring tonight. Pressure is the payload of the scam.
A greeting that is too warm and too general, combined with an urgent request. This combination is nearly always a scam.
A QR code to scan, a shortened link, or an attachment you were not expecting. These are delivery mechanisms, not neutral tools.

sections.body:
The delivery method tells you which checks matter, and many people check the wrong thing.

Email is the classic channel. Attackers can put any display name and any subject they like. What you can check is the real sending domain, whether your actual account sent the message, and where any link really goes.

SMS and **WhatsApp or Zalo** are used for short, urgent pretexts, because they feel personal and arrive on the phone you are holding. The check that matters is the number, and whether you had any relationship with it. SMS sender numbers can be spoofed, so an official-looking short code still needs verifying.

A phone call is used for authority and for urgency together. Caller names can be faked. A claimed bank, a claimed police or tax office, a claimed tech support line offering to "fix" your computer. The one rule that matters: hang up and call the organisation on a number you already had.

Social media messages are used for the impersonation pattern, because a compromised or cloned account of a friend is very hard to spot. The check is the same: verify through a different channel. A message from a friend asking for money or a code is the classic pattern, and it is one of the most common in every country.

Marketplace and delivery listings are used to draw you to a fake payment page. The check is the address of the site, and whether you arrived there by clicking or by typing it yourself.

Search results and adverts are used to place a fraudulent site at the top. The check is the spelling of the domain, read one character at a time.

Notice the pattern in the channel list. In every case, the correct verification is the same: use a channel you chose yourself, not one the message gave you. The message's phone number, its link, its email address and its app are all under the sender's control. Your card, your bank's website, the number in your own contacts, and your bank's app are not.
examples: It was from my friend's number, so I called my friend on the number I already had.
I hung up and called the bank's number on the back of my card.
I typed the website address myself instead of using the link in the message.
sections.heading: How the message gets to you, and why that changes what you check

sections.body: Stop the moment you notice a second signal. Not the third, not the fifth. The second. A message that fails one check has an explanation: a typo, a strange format, an unusual but possible request. A message that fails two checks is a scam with very high probability, and every additional minute of reading it is time the scammer is spending on you. Put the phone down, do not reply, and do not click anything to "have a look". Opening a link can start the attack without you entering anything, and replying confirms that the number or address is live. If you have already replied, that is not a disaster, but it is the moment to stop and use the procedure in the next section.
sections.heading: The moment to stop

sections.body:
These steps are in order, and speed matters more than completeness. Do them in this sequence.

First, **disconnect from the action**: close the page, do not enter anything else, and if you installed something, stop using that device for now.

Second, **call the organisation using a number you already had**. If it was your bank, use the number on your card. If it was a marketplace, use the app. Say: "I think I have been scammed, here is what happened".

Third, **if you paid, ask for the payment to be reversed**. With cards, banks can often freeze a transaction and raise a chargeback. With bank transfers, the request is time-critical, because the money may be moved onward within hours. With gift cards and cryptocurrency, recovery is usually not possible, which is why the prevention in the next section is so valuable.

Fourth, **change the exposed credentials from a different device**. If you entered a password on a fake page, change that password, and change it from a device that is not the one you used. If you entered a one-time code, the attacker may already be logged in; change the password, end the other sessions, and tell the bank.

Fifth, **tell the people around you**. Scammers reuse details, and a message that reached you may reach your family from a compromised account of yours. One message to the family group removes a whole family of risk.

Sixth, **keep the evidence**. Screenshots of the message, the sender, the payment reference and the time. The bank, the platform and the police will all ask for it, and it is much harder to recover from after the fact.
examples: I called the number on the back of my card, not the one in the message.
I changed the password on my laptop, because the phone might still be compromised.
I sent the screenshot to my family so they would not answer if it reached them too.
sections.heading: What to do in the first ten minutes after a click or a payment
steps: Close the page and stop using the device if you installed anything.
Call the organisation on a number you already had.
Ask for the payment to be reversed, and do it fast.
Change the exposed password from a different device.
Tell your family, because the same message may reach them.

sections.body:
These are the terms used in bank guidance, in police notices and in the news. Knowing them lets you look up the right advice for the problem in front of you.

Phishing is a fraudulent message, usually by email, designed to steal credentials or money.

Smishing is the same thing by text message.

Vishing is the same thing by voice call.

Spoofing is presenting a false sender identity, so a call or a message appears to come from a number or an address that belongs to someone else.

Malware is software installed on your device, usually to steal information or to give an attacker control.

One-time code is the short number a bank sends to confirm a login or a payment. Anyone who has it can complete the action.

Credential stuffing is a technique where stolen passwords from one service are tried against many others, which is why reusing a password is so risky.

Mule account is a bank account used to receive and pass on criminal money, often opened by an individual who believes they are helping a company or a cause.

Chargeback is a reversal of a card payment requested from the bank, usually because the transaction was not authorised or the goods never arrived.

Advance fee is money demanded before a service is delivered. It is the oldest scam in the book and it is now often used in fake job offers and fake investments.
sections.heading: The words of fraud, one by one

terms.example: That email about a locked account was phishing, and it used our bank's real logo.
terms.gloss: A fraudulent message, usually by email, designed to steal credentials or money by pretending to be someone you trust.

terms.example: The message about a parcel was smishing, and the link was not the courier's website.
terms.gloss: Phishing carried out by text message. Short, urgent, and arriving on the phone you are holding.

terms.example: They called pretending to be the tax office. That is vishing, and I hung up and called the real number.
terms.gloss: Phishing carried out by a phone call, usually with a claim of authority from a bank, a police force or a support line.

terms.example: The message showed my brother's name, but the number was spoofed.
terms.gloss: Presenting a false sender identity so that a call or a message appears to come from a number or address that belongs to someone else.

terms.example: I gave them the one-time code, and that was the moment the account was theirs.
terms.gloss: The short number a bank sends to confirm a login or a payment. Anyone who holds it can complete the action.

terms.example: They asked me to receive money and pass it on. That makes my account a mule account and the money is stolen.
terms.gloss: A bank account used to receive and pass on criminal money, sometimes opened by someone who believes they are helping a company or a cause.

terms.example: The bank raised a chargeback and returned the money five days later.
terms.gloss: A reversal of a card payment requested from the bank, usually because the transaction was not authorised or the goods never arrived.

terms.example: They wanted a small fee before the equipment arrived, and then a larger one.
terms.gloss: Money demanded before a service is delivered. Common in fake job offers, fake investments and fake love interests.

sections.body:
Prevention is much cheaper than recovery, and the strongest prevention available is choosing a payment method that can be reversed. Not all money is equally hard to lose.

Card payments are the most reversible. A bank can often freeze a transaction while it is pending, and it can raise a chargeback afterwards. If you have paid by card, contact the bank immediately. Do not wait for the statement.

Bank transfers are much harder. In many countries a transfer to an unfamiliar account cannot be reversed once it has been made, and the money may be moved onward within hours. In Vietnam, transfers through the banking network are generally final once completed, which is exactly why fraudsters push you to transfer rather than to pay by card. The rule for transfers is simple: never transfer to someone you have not verified in person or by a call on a number you already had.

Payment apps and instant transfers sit between the two. The institution can often freeze an account, but it needs to act fast. This is the strongest argument for the first-ten-minutes procedure: speed is the thing that decides whether money comes back.

Gift cards and vouchers are effectively unrecoverable. Anyone can buy one and anyone can spend it, and no institution has a duty to trace it. If a message asks you to buy gift cards, that is a scam with no ambiguity, and you should end the conversation.

Cryptocurrency is unrecoverable by design. The network does not reverse payments, the recipient is anonymous in practice, and exchanges will not help a police request from another country. Treat any request to send crypto as the final signal, not the first one.

Cash through an intermediary is a pattern worth naming. If someone asks you to meet a courier and hand over cash, the money is stolen, and you will be the one left explaining it. This also puts you at risk of being charged with handling stolen goods, which is a very serious matter in every jurisdiction.
examples: I paid by card, so I called the bank straight away and they froze it.
A transfer to an account I had never seen is not something I will do over the phone.
They wanted gift cards, and I ended the conversation there.
sections.heading: Payment methods, and which ones can be undone

sections.body:
Two groups are targeted with different scripts, and both scripts are worth knowing in advance.

Scams aimed at **older relatives** usually impersonate a family member, a bank, or a delivery company. The family member message is the cruel one: a new phone number, a plea for money, a promise to pay back. It works because the message arrives during the one part of the day when the target is alone and rushed.

The defences are practical and family-level, not technical. Agree a family code word that only the family uses, for situations like this. Set a rule that any request for money gets verified by a second channel, even when the sender seems familiar. And make it normal for the older relative to call you before doing anything, so that verification does not feel like suspicion.

Scams aimed at **small businesses** are about invoices, payroll and suppliers. A fake invoice with real bank details arrives from a supplier whose email has been compromised. A supplier changes their bank account for one payment. A payroll email asks an employee to change the account that their salary is paid into. A government letter threatens a fine for an unpaid registration.

The defences are mostly process, and they are cheap. Confirm any change of bank details by phone using the number you already hold, never the one in the message. Make one named person responsible for payment changes, so the request cannot be processed by whoever is closest to the inbox. Tell the whole team, including the newest person, because new employees are the ones who feel least able to question a request. And keep a list of known suppliers with their verified bank details, so a change request has something to be compared against.

In both cases the pattern is the same: the request arrives from a trusted identity, it asks you to move to a new channel, and it needs to be settled today. A process that stops the channel change stops the scam.
examples: We agreed a code word, so a message about an emergency can be checked in one call.
Confirm any change of bank details by calling the number we already had on file.
New staff get told about this on day one, because they are the ones who find it hardest to question a request.
sections.heading: The scams that target older relatives and small businesses

sections.body: These sentences do two jobs: they end the conversation with the scammer without engaging, and they keep you steady with the people around you. Use them as they are, and change the detail to fit your situation.
examples: I will call the number on my card myself. Thank you.
I do not make decisions about money on the phone.
Hang up and call me back on your usual number.
I do not need to act on this today. Nothing legitimate expires in ten minutes.
Check with a second channel before you pay anything.
Do not send codes, pin numbers or passwords to anyone, including me.
I am going to read this to my sister before I do anything.
If it were real, it would still be real in an hour.
sections.heading: Sentences you can reuse when a scam comes

sections.body: The people who rarely get scammed are not the clever ones. They have a routine. Set up your account so that unexpected requests cannot succeed: a strong unique password for your email first, because email is the account that can reset all the others, then multi-factor authentication on banking, then on the accounts that hold money. Turn off SMS two-factor codes where an authenticator app or a hardware key is available, because SMS is the channel scammers can take over. Check once a month which of your accounts have your phone number or email address attached, and remove the ones you no longer use. Set a spending limit or a separate account for everyday money. And agree the family code word. None of this makes you invulnerable. It makes the ten minutes a scammer needs harder, and that is the whole game.
sections.heading: Building a routine that stops scams before they start

item.summary: Scam messages are built on a small number of patterns, and those patterns leave signals you can learn to read in seconds. After reading this you can recognise the four structures behind almost every scam, spot the tells in a message before you act, run the first-ten-minutes procedure after an incident, choose payment methods that can be reversed, and say the sentences that stop a scammer without alarming the people around you.
item.title: How to Spot Online Scams and Fake Messages
